context.title: Why is the sky blue, and why are leaves green?

sections.heading: Different interactions with the same sunlight
paragraphs: The blue sky and a green leaf illustrate two different ways that matter changes the light reaching our eyes. Sunlight contains a broad range of wavelengths. The colour we perceive depends on which wavelengths reach us, their relative intensities, and our visual sensitivity.

sections.heading: Why air makes the sky appear blue
paragraphs: Sunlight’s oscillating electric field induces oscillations in the charges within air molecules. These produce radiation in other directions: light is scattered. For molecules much smaller than the wavelength, Rayleigh scattering applies, with scattering strength approximately proportional to 1/λ⁴.

Consequently, 450 nm blue light is scattered about 4.4 times more strongly than 650 nm red light under the same conditions. When we look away from the Sun, some of this scattered sunlight reaches our eyes, enriched in shorter wavelengths. Rayleigh scattering changes the light’s direction while essentially preserving its wavelength. It does not convert red photons into blue photons.

sections.heading: Blue rather than violet, and the different colours of sunset
paragraphs: Violet scatters even more strongly, but perceived colour depends on the entire scattered spectrum and the eye’s response. Our lower sensitivity to violet helps explain the blue appearance.

At sunset, sunlight travels through a longer atmospheric path. More short-wavelength light is scattered out of the direct beam, leaving the transmitted sunlight relatively enriched in red and orange. The observer’s viewing direction therefore matters: scattered skylight and the direct solar beam have different spectra.

sections.heading: Why a leaf appears green
paragraphs: Chlorophyll’s molecular structure gives it wavelength-dependent absorption bands, with strong absorption in the blue and red regions and weaker absorption in much of the green region. Absorption transfers photon energy into an electronic excitation of the pigment. The surrounding protein also influences these absorption properties.

sections.heading: Pigment chemistry and tissue structure
paragraphs: A whole leaf combines this selective absorption with reflection, transmission and internal scattering. Light changes direction at interfaces within the tissue, including those between hydrated cell walls and air spaces. Some light escapes back towards the observer. Because pigments remove blue and red light more strongly, the escaping visible light is relatively enriched in green. Leaf colour therefore reflects both pigment chemistry and tissue structure.

sections.heading: A green appearance does not mean most green light is rejected
paragraphs: A leaf can absorb substantial green light while reflecting more green than blue or red. Weaker absorption also allows green light to penetrate deeper before absorption. Under strong white light, this can deliver additional excitation to deeper chloroplasts whose photosynthetic capacity is less saturated than that of chloroplasts near the illuminated surface.
Terashima and colleagues demonstrated this advantage for additional green light in sunflower leaves; it depends on the background illumination.

sections.heading: Sunlight and human vision
paragraphs: Sunlight supplies both energy and information to life. It contains a broad range of wavelengths; a prism separates its visible components into a continuous spectrum from violet to red. Human eyes detect roughly 380–780 nm, using this light to recognise objects, colours and movement. This is the human visible range.

sections.heading: Photosynthetically active radiation
paragraphs: Plants capture energy from an overlapping part of the spectrum. Photosynthetically active radiation—PAR—is conventionally defined as 400–700 nm, encompassing blue, green and red light. Photosynthetic pigments absorb photons within this range to drive the light reactions. PAR gives us a common basis for measuring light available for photosynthesis; the amount actually absorbed depends on the pigments and the leaf.

sections.heading: Far-red light beyond conventional PAR
paragraphs: Biological activity continues beyond these boundaries. Far-red photons around 700–750 nm can support photosynthesis alongside shorter-wavelength light, illustrating why conventional PAR is a measurement range rather than a strict limit on photosynthesis.

sections.heading: Ultraviolet, infrared and microwaves
paragraphs: Toward shorter wavelengths, ultraviolet can trigger protective responses and damage cells at excessive exposure. Toward longer wavelengths, absorbed infrared contributes to warming tissues. Microwaves lie farther beyond infrared; their absorption by water and other molecules provides the familiar example of heating food. Different parts of the spectrum therefore interact with living material in different ways.

sections.heading: Photon energy
paragraphs: Light carries energy in discrete packets called photons. Einstein’s 1905 light-quantum proposal connects each photon’s energy to its frequency: E = hν = hc/λ, where h is Planck’s constant, c is the speed of light and λ is wavelength. Shorter wavelengths therefore carry more energy per photon: a blue photon carries more than a red photon. Increasing light intensity at a fixed wavelength supplies more photons without changing each photon’s energy. This distinction matters when comparing the energy supplied by different colours.

sections.heading: Rayleigh scattering
paragraphs: Wavelength also affects how light is scattered. Light’s electric field makes charges within air molecules oscillate, producing radiation in other directions. Rayleigh scattering increases approximately as 1/λ⁴, so blue light is scattered much more strongly than red. This wavelength dependence comes from the molecules’ electromagnetic response; greater photon energy alone does not explain it. Scattering changes the photon’s direction while essentially preserving its wavelength.

sections.heading: The blue sky and sunset

sections.heading: Selective absorption and leaf colour
paragraphs: Light reaching a leaf can be absorbed, reflected or transmitted. Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red light strongly, but green light more weakly. Consequently, the reflected light is relatively enriched in green, giving leaves their familiar colour. Green appearance does not mean that most green light is reflected.

sections.heading: Different pigments, different absorption spectra
paragraphs: The pigments have different absorption spectra. Chlorophyll a and b have shifted blue and red absorption peaks, so their contributions overlap without being identical. Carotenoids absorb mainly in the blue to blue-green region, extending light capture. Peak positions also depend on the pigment’s molecular environment.

sections.heading: Green light inside a leaf
paragraphs: Green light still supports photosynthesis. Its weaker absorption lets it penetrate deeper into the leaf, while internal scattering lengthens its path and increases opportunities for absorption. Under strong white light, additional green light can reach deeper chloroplasts whose photosynthesis is less saturated, making it more effective than additional red light. Leaf anatomy and pigment distribution matter; thickness alone does not guarantee this advantage.

sections.heading: Accessory pigments in algae
paragraphs: Other photosynthetic organisms use different pigment combinations. In the red alga Griffithsia pacifica, phycoerythrin absorbs strongly around 540 and 565 nm, capturing green wavelengths that chlorophyll absorbs relatively weakly. These wavelengths are within conventional PAR: the contrast is between pigment absorption spectra.

sections.heading: Why chlorophyll a and b absorb differently
paragraphs: Chlorophyll a and b absorb different wavelengths because their molecular structures differ. Chlorophyll b has a formyl group (–CHO) where a has a methyl group (–CH₃). This changes the electron distribution and the energy gaps that photons must match. Surrounding protein charges also affect these gaps, so the same pigment can absorb differently in different protein environments.

sections.heading: Complementary absorption and different roles
paragraphs: Their absorption spectra complement each other. Chlorophyll b broadens light collection and generally transfers excitation to lower-energy chlorophyll a states. In land plants, chlorophyll a also supplies the principal donor pigments for reaction-centre photochemistry.

sections.heading: Organisation enables excitation transfer
paragraphs: To make these pigments work together, proteins organise them into light-harvesting complexes. The proteins control pigment spacing, orientation and excitation energies, allowing rapid transfer towards a reaction centre. During antenna transfer, excitation moves between pigments; there is no net electron transfer between them. Electron transfer and charge separation occur when the reaction centre performs photochemistry.

sections.heading: LHCII and LHCI in land plants
paragraphs: LHCII mainly supplies photosystem II and usually forms a trimer of three proteins. Each protein binds 8 chlorophyll a, 6 chlorophyll b and 4 carotenoids. Its chlorophyll a:b ratio is approximately 1.3.

LHCI supplies photosystem I and usually consists of four proteins beside the PSI core. The whole belt in one pea structure contains 45 chlorophyll a, 12 chlorophyll b and 13 carotenoids. Its chlorophyll a:b ratio is approximately 3.7–3.8.
LHCII is called the major antenna because its numerous copies bind a large fraction of plant chlorophyll. PSI also contains a substantial chlorophyll-a-rich core antenna.

sections.heading: What the pigment ratios imply
paragraphs: The pigment ratios have functional consequences. LHCII’s greater proportion of chlorophyll b strengthens complementary absorption. LHCI contains proportionally more a, including specially coupled pairs that create low-energy “red forms” absorbing beyond 700 nm. These arise from pigment arrangement and protein interactions, not from the ratio alone. Some require thermally assisted uphill transfer to reach the reaction centre: extending spectral capture can therefore slow trapping.

sections.heading: Two experiments, two discoveries
paragraphs: Two experiments connect this organisation to its discovery. Emerson and Arnold’s 1932 flash experiments helped establish that many chlorophyll molecules cooperate within a photosynthetic unit. Emerson enhancement in 1957 showed that red and far-red light together could produce more photosynthesis than the sum of their separate effects. The first supports collective light harvesting; the second helped reveal two cooperating light reactions, leading into how PSII and PSI drive electron transport together.

context.heading: Two photosystems in one membrane
paragraphs: The light reactions take place in the thylakoid membrane. The aqueous space inside is the lumen; the space outside is the stroma, where carbon assimilation occurs. The membrane allows electron transport to establish a proton gradient between these two spaces.

Both PSII and PSI receive excitation from their antennas. Their reaction-centre chlorophyll a cofactors are embedded in different protein environments, giving them different electron-transfer properties. P680 and P700 are historical spectroscopic names associated with their donor systems, near 680 and 700 nm; they are not two entirely different chlorophyll molecules.

context.heading: An excitation becomes a redox event
paragraphs: In an antenna, one pigment's excitation can be passed to another without a net electron moving along the antenna chain. In a reaction centre, an excited donor transfers an electron to an acceptor. The donor is left oxidised and the acceptor reduced: charge has been separated. Subsequent transfers help stabilise that separation instead of allowing immediate recombination.

To repeat the reaction, the oxidised donor must receive a replacement electron and the reduced acceptor must pass its electron onward. These requirements connect the two photosystems to the rest of metabolism. PSII ultimately draws replacement electrons from water; PSI receives them through the intersystem carriers and can reduce ferredoxin.
Both photosystems can be excited at the same time. Their cooperation is a connection between electron transfers, not a timetable in which PSI waits for all PSII reactions to finish.

context.heading: One reaction links photosynthesis to the oxygen we breathe
paragraphs: On the lumen side of PSII, the oxygen-evolving complex contains a manganese–calcium cluster that accumulates oxidising equivalents over successive photochemical turnovers. Through a redox-active tyrosine, it supplies electrons that replace those removed from the PSII donor system.

The net water-oxidation reaction is 2 H₂O → O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻. Producing one O₂ therefore requires four successful PSII photochemical turnovers. The four protons are released into the lumen; the four electrons enter the transport chain. Water is not split simply because a free water molecule absorbs sunlight.

context.heading: The oxygen comes from water
paragraphs: The O₂ released in oxygenic photosynthesis comes from water, not from the oxygen atoms of the incoming CO₂. Isotope experiments make this distinction visible: oxygen labelled in water can be traced into the evolved O₂.

That molecular by-product has a planetary consequence. Oxygenic photosynthesis supplies O₂ for aerobic respiration in animals, plants, fungi and many microbes. The same light-driven event provides electrons for reducing carbon and an oxidant that other organisms—and the plant itself—can use in respiration.

context.heading: Why the textbook route begins with PSII
paragraphs: The familiar sequence—water → PSII → plastoquinone → cytochrome b₆f → plastocyanin → PSI → ferredoxin → NADP⁺—describes net electron flow from a source to a sink. It begins at PSII because that is where electrons from water enter this route. It does not describe the order in which sunlight first reaches the photosystems.

Both photosystems absorb photons concurrently. PSII photochemistry makes water-derived electrons available to the intersystem chain. After passage through carriers, PSI uses a second excitation to reduce ferredoxin. Ferredoxin–NADP⁺ reductase, FNR, transfers reducing equivalents to NADP⁺: two electrons are required per NADPH.

context.heading: Two energy boosts explain the cooperation
paragraphs: The Z-scheme is an energy/redox view of this same membrane pathway. Its two light-driven boosts explain why red and far-red illumination can cooperate: the systems act in series in net electron transfer. The drawing is not a map of vertical positions in the chloroplast or a film of a single photon travelling from PSII to PSI.

For four electrons delivered from water to NADP⁺, the ideal minimum is four successful excitations in PSII and four in PSI. The outputs are one O₂ and two NADPH, while proton movements along the route also help establish the force for ATP synthesis. Actual leaves require more incident photons because not every photon is absorbed or produces productive photochemistry.

study: Water → PSII → PQ → b₆f → PC → PSI → Fd/FNR → NADP⁺.
Both photosystems absorb light; 'linear' describes the net source-to-sink route.
Ideal minimum: 8 productive photons → 4 transferred e⁻ → 1 O₂ + 2 NADPH.

history.title: The Z-scheme resolves the two-light puzzle
history.body: Hill and Bendall's 1960 working hypothesis linked two light reactions with electron carriers. The historical point is the connection between two energy inputs, not memorising a zigzag shape.

evidence.point: The linear pathway remains a sound reference route within a regulated, branched electron-transport system.
evidence.scope: Establish it before adding branches. A recent review does not make the foundational route obsolete.

illustration.static: One membrane pathway and a small aligned Z-scheme use the same carrier order and two light-input marks. Use clear source/sink arrows and distinguish electron transport from excitation transfer.
illustration.animation: A 30–40 second segment of the shared membrane animation should illuminate PSII and PSI together, then highlight the net source-to-sink path. Leave the full path visible on the static slide.
illustration.priority: High as part of the shared membrane animation

optional: No detailed redox-potential scale or complete carrier cofactor list is needed.
Students should recognise the role of mobile carriers rather than memorise every abbreviation without a diagram.
drafts.bridgeOut: Electron flow also moves protons. Show how a membrane gradient converts these transfers into ATP.

drafts.title: A proton gradient powers ATP synthesis
drafts.bridgeIn: The electron pathway supplies reductant; proton coupling explains its second energy output.
drafts.takeaway: Electron flow builds proton motive force; ATP synthase uses it to make ATP in the stroma.

context.heading: Build a gradient, then use it
paragraphs: Water oxidation releases H⁺ into the lumen. Plastoquinone picks up electrons and stromal protons, and cytochrome b₆f processes quinol through its Q cycle, producing additional net proton transfer towards the lumen. A membrane that restricts free proton leakage allows this process to build proton motive force.

Proton motive force has both a chemical component, the pH difference, and an electrical component, the membrane potential. Protons returning from the lumen to the stroma through ATP synthase drive rotary catalysis of ADP + phosphate to ATP. The catalytic head faces the stroma, so ATP becomes available on the same side as NADPH and the Calvin–Benson–Bassham cycle.

context.heading: One consistent ideal budget
paragraphs: For four electrons in linear flow, a full b₆f Q cycle gives a convenient account: 4 H⁺ from water oxidation plus 8 H⁺ transferred through PQ/b₆f accounting, making 12 lumen-side protons. The PQ proton contribution is already included; counting it again would overestimate the yield.

A plant chloroplast ATP synthase with a c₁₄ ring couples a full rotation to 14 translocated H⁺ and three ATP. Under ideal tight coupling, 12 H⁺ therefore support 12 × 3/14 ≈ 2.57 ATP, alongside two NADPH. This is a stoichiometric average under stated assumptions, not a promise that every leaf always makes exactly that ATP amount. Stromal H⁺ consumed in NADPH formation affects proton balance but is not another independently pumped batch of lumen protons.

study: H⁺ accumulates in the lumen; ATP is formed on the stromal side.
pmf = a pH difference + an electrical potential.
Illustrative budget per 4 e⁻: 12 H⁺ → approximately 2.57 ATP, using H⁺/ATP = 14/3.

history.title: ATP in the dark from an imposed pH difference
history.body: Jagendorf and Uribe acidified chloroplast preparations, then imposed an acid-to-base transition with ADP and phosphate. ATP formation without illumination showed that a proton gradient can be the immediate energy source; light normally builds that gradient.

evidence.point: Recent work emphasises regulation of ATP synthase conductivity as well as proton supply. A 2026 study proposes a PGR5-dependent brake on ATP synthase under high irradiance.
evidence.scope: An evolving regulatory interpretation; do not label PGR5 as an established proton pump or a uniquely identified Fd–PQ reductase.

illustration.static: Reuse the same lumen/stroma membrane. Mark the two proton sources, ATP synthase's return path and stromal ATP output. Keep one small 4 + 8 = 12 proton account; no slide filled only with equations.
illustration.animation: A 30-second proton-flow and ATP-synthase segment completes the shared membrane animation. The acid/base experiment can be two static frames rather than another animation.
illustration.priority: High as part of the shared animation

optional: The detailed Q-cycle branch chemistry stays in Context.
Structural coupling and effective coupling inferred in vivo are different kinds of estimate; alternative assumptions belong in the accounting note.
drafts.bridgeOut: The membrane can make both ATP and reductant. Can changing the electron route change their relative supply?

drafts.title: Electron routes make the system flexible
drafts.bridgeIn: Linear flow provides a reference ATP/reductant supply. Metabolism does not always demand those outputs in the same proportion.
drafts.takeaway: Electron routing changes proton flow, reductant output and protection; its use depends on the state of the system.

context.heading: Three useful route families
paragraphs: Linear flow takes new electrons from water to NADP⁺. It produces NADPH and contributes proton motive force. Cyclic flow returns electrons from the PSI acceptor side towards the plastoquinone/b₆f pathway and back to PSI. It can support proton motive force without making net NADPH or evolving net O₂ through that cycle.

Oxygen-directed flow provides another outlet: electrons ultimately reduce O₂, so reducing equivalents are removed rather than retained as net NADPH. In a complete water–water cycle, gross O₂ production at PSII can be balanced by O₂ uptake downstream. Classical Mehler chemistry produces reactive oxygen intermediates that must be detoxified; flavodiiron proteins provide a distinct O₂-reduction route in several photosynthetic lineages. Native angiosperms lack the photosynthetic FLV system, so these routes must not be drawn as interchangeable universal leaf components.

context.heading: Which route runs, and why?
paragraphs: There is no fixed ranking that the leaf follows in every condition. When NADP⁺ is regenerated by carbon metabolism, linear delivery to that sink can proceed. When downstream acceptors become reduced—for example during a rapid increase in illumination before metabolism catches up—proton regulation, alternative sinks and restricted electron delivery become important.

Cyclic flow recirculates electrons and can increase proton coupling without adding net reductant; it does not, by itself, dispose of a stock of excess electrons. An O₂-directed outlet does remove reducing equivalents. Their relative activities follow acceptor availability, redox state, enzyme regulation and proton motive force. Several routes can operate simultaneously.

context.heading: Yield requires a route and an assumption
paragraphs: With a full b₆f Q cycle and H⁺/ATP = 14/3, the four-electron linear example gives eight productive photons, two NADPH and approximately 2.57 ATP. Four turns through a non-proton-pumping cyclic return require four PSI photons and supply eight translocated H⁺, corresponding ideally to approximately 1.71 ATP with no net NADPH. An NDH-mediated return can add proton pumping, so it has a different coupling account.

These are ideal yields per absorbed, productive photochemical event, not measured leaf quantum yields or percentages of solar energy captured. Metabolic ATP demand, ATP concentration and ATP production flux are also different quantities: recent evidence argues against claiming that every C₃ leaf must use one fixed cyclic fraction to fill an inevitable ATP deficit.

study: Linear: water → NADP⁺; net NADPH + proton coupling.
Cyclic: electrons return to PSI; proton coupling without net NADPH.
O₂ outlet: reducing equivalents consumed; proton coupling may continue.
Route use depends on redox state and available sinks; no fixed universal priority.

history.title: The historical linear diagram becomes a network
history.body: Keep the Z-scheme as the reference route, then add one return arrow and one terminal outlet. This is a conceptual extension, not a replacement discovery story.

evidence.point: In Arabidopsis cyclic-flow mutants, Degen and colleagues found lower pmf with maintained chloroplast MgATP²⁻ levels.
evidence.scope: A pool measurement challenges an obligatory top-up argument but does not measure ATP synthesis flux or show that cyclic routes have no energetic function.

evidence.point: Flaveria bidentis studies connect cyclic pathways with growth and PSI protection, while heterologous FLV in tobacco can compete with cyclic routing.
evidence.scope: C₄ knockdowns and engineered tobacco are different systems. Neither establishes a universal route priority for an ordinary C₃ leaf.

illustration.static: A shared membrane network with only three highlighted route families, plus a compact input/output comparison. The detailed NDH and water–water arithmetic remains in the expandable accounting note.
illustration.animation: Optional 20-second route toggles reuse the membrane scene. Do not animate several coloured streams at once; each toggle must leave its net output visible.
illustration.priority: Secondary extension to the shared animation

optional: Instructor note includes NDH: approximately 16 H⁺/4 circuits → 3.43 ATP under the pumping model.
Malate export and other metabolic sinks are reserve context, not another list for students.
Detailed PGR5/PGRL1 mechanisms remain under active investigation.
drafts.bridgeOut: Routing regulates what happens to electrons after charge separation. Protection can also act earlier, on the excitation itself.

drafts.title: Three fates of an excitation
drafts.bridgeIn: The electron routes described successful charge separation. Absorbed excitation can also leave by other pathways.
drafts.takeaway: Photochemistry, fluorescence and heat dissipation compete for excitation energy.

context.heading: Absorption does not guarantee photochemistry
paragraphs: After absorption and rapid relaxation within a pigment, excitation may reach a reaction centre and support charge separation. It may instead be lost by non-radiative relaxation, appearing as heat, or by emission of a fluorescence photon. In a leaf, chlorophyll fluorescence is predominantly red and far-red; some absorbed energy has already been lost before emission.

These pathways compete. If productive reaction centres become unavailable, excitation has less opportunity to drive photochemistry. Fluorescence can rise, but it need not: an increase in heat dissipation can lower fluorescence at the same time. A weak fluorescence signal therefore does not automatically mean efficient photosynthesis.
The key distinction is between the amount of light absorbed and the fraction used productively. The leaf cannot avoid every absorption event, but it can regulate the subsequent fate of excitation.

study: Absorbed excitation → photochemistry, fluorescence or heat.
Fluorescence reports competition between pathways, not carbon fixation directly.
Regulated heat dissipation provides protection before damaging reactions occur.

history.title: The fluorescence signal changes while the light stays on
history.body: Kautsky's fluorescence transient shows that a leaf's internal state changes after illumination. The same light input can produce a changing fluorescence output as photochemistry and dissipation change.
history.priority: Optional; useful link to the later measurement slide

evidence.point: Modern NPQ work treats fluorescence as a readout of competing decay processes, while investigating where and how additional quenching arises.
evidence.scope: Do not identify low fluorescence with a unique mechanism.

illustration.static: One excitation-state sketch branching to reaction-centre photochemistry, red fluorescence and heat. Keep the three labelled paths visible; avoid a detailed quantum energy-level diagram.
illustration.animation: None needed.

optional: Triplet chlorophyll and singlet oxygen can be named as the risk behind protection, without adding a separate spin-state lecture.
drafts.bridgeOut: Lumen acidification now gives us the trigger for increasing the heat-dissipation branch.

drafts.title: Too much excitation: protect the system
drafts.bridgeIn: The proton gradient stores usable energy and also signals when absorbed excitation is outpacing its use.
drafts.takeaway: Lumen acidification coordinates heat dissipation and electron-flow control to protect photosynthesis.

context.heading: A feedback from the lumen to the antenna
paragraphs: If light absorption exceeds the rate at which downstream chemistry can use its products, reaction centres and electron acceptors become increasingly constrained. Long-lived excited states and inappropriate electron transfers can generate reactive oxygen species and damage the photosynthetic apparatus.

A falling lumen pH helps activate the rapidly reversible, energy-dependent part of non-photochemical quenching, qE. Protonation changes the behaviour of PsbS and favours antenna states that dissipate excitation as heat. This uses the proton-gradient concept already established; it is not an unrelated protective switch.

context.heading: The xanthophyll cycle supports the response
paragraphs: Acidification also activates violaxanthin de-epoxidase on the lumen side, promoting conversion of violaxanthin through antheraxanthin to zeaxanthin. These pigment changes help establish and maintain protective quenching states. When excitation pressure falls, quenching can relax and zeaxanthin can be epoxidised back.

The central message is coordinated regulation: the same antenna that captures excitation can change its probability of dissipating it. Zeaxanthin is not simply a sunscreen that prevents all photons entering, and PsbS is not another chlorophyll antenna transferring captured light to the reaction centre.

Lumen acidification also restricts electron delivery through cytochrome b₆f, helping protect PSI when its acceptor side is constrained. Dissipating excitation and regulating electron flow act at different points in the same system. If damage nevertheless occurs, repair—such as replacement of damaged PSII D1 protein—is a separate response.

study: Lumen H⁺ rises → PsbS/antenna response → more excitation lost safely as heat.
Violaxanthin ⇄ antheraxanthin ⇄ zeaxanthin.
Protection must engage and relax; damage repair is a separate process.

history.title: Return to the ATP-in-the-dark experiment
history.body: The gradient introduced through chemiosmosis now has a second role: it coordinates protection. Reusing that concept is more valuable than introducing another historical biography.

evidence.point: The 2025 synthesis proposes a PsbS-triggered antenna conformational switch, with zeaxanthin extending the domain that can be quenched.
evidence.scope: A working model within a field with unresolved molecular mechanisms; teach the physiological chain more firmly than one quenching-site explanation.

evidence.point: A 2026 Arabidopsis study attributes most measured NPQ to LHCII, linking protection directly back to the earlier antenna slide.
evidence.scope: Compartment estimates depend on the mutant comparisons and fluorescence analysis; do not print a universal percentage.

illustration.static: Reuse the same membrane and lumen. Link acidification to a small PsbS/antenna inset and the three xanthophyll names. A static before/after pair must show the full causal sequence without playback.
illustration.animation: A 30–45 second overlay changes lumen pH, the antenna's heat branch and the xanthophyll state. Use the same membrane scene; no new visual vocabulary.
illustration.priority: High: a causal sequence that benefits from animation

optional: State transitions redistribute antenna excitation between photosystems; keep them to one optional sentence and distinguish them from qE.
D1 repair and delayed NPQ relaxation are removable examples, not additional full slides.
Ascorbate dependence of violaxanthin de-epoxidase stays in instructor notes.
drafts.bridgeOut: These changes alter fluorescence. A controlled measurement can separate operating photochemistry from some of the competing losses.

drafts.title: Reading photosynthesis through fluorescence
drafts.bridgeIn: Fluorescence changes with reaction-centre availability and heat dissipation; measuring it requires a defined light protocol.
drafts.takeaway: Fluorescence estimates PSII photochemical performance, not ATP production or CO₂ uptake directly.

context.heading: Compare a defined minimum and maximum
paragraphs: A saturating pulse briefly closes available PSII photochemical traps, allowing comparison with the fluorescence before the pulse. After suitable dark adaptation, Fᵥ/Fₘ = (Fₘ − Fₒ)/Fₘ estimates the maximum efficiency of PSII photochemistry. During illumination, ΦPSII = (Fₘ′ − Fₛ)/Fₘ′ estimates its operating yield.

These quantities answer different questions. A well-performing dark-adapted PSII population can operate at a lower yield in the light because of reaction-centre closure and regulated dissipation. A low operating yield is not by itself proof of irreversible damage.

Multiplying ΦPSII by absorbed photon flux and the fraction delivered to PSII gives an estimate of PSII electron flow. Leaf absorptance and excitation allocation must be known or assumed. Alternative electron sinks, cyclic PSI flow and downstream metabolism mean this estimate cannot simply be relabelled ATP production, NADPH production or net CO₂ assimilation.

study: Dark-adapted maximum: Fᵥ/Fₘ.
Operating PSII yield: (Fₘ′ − Fₛ)/Fₘ′.
Estimated PSII ETR ≠ net CO₂ assimilation or ATP flux.

history.title: From the Kautsky transient to a controlled probe
history.body: The changing fluorescence signal becomes informative when the illumination protocol is controlled. A single trace is enough to connect the historical observation to measurement.

evidence.point: Recent routing studies reinforce the need to keep PSII electron flow, PSI cycling and the carbon-directed electron supply distinct.
evidence.scope: The lecture does not attempt to infer cyclic flow by casually subtracting noisy PSI and PSII measurements.

illustration.static: One small fluorescence trace with the measuring point and saturating pulse labelled. Put each yield beside its experimental state, not in a wall of equations.
illustration.animation: None needed.

optional: The frequently cited Fᵥ/Fₘ value near 0.83 is a useful reference for many unstressed leaves, not a universal diagnostic threshold.
NPQ parameter definitions and pulse-instrument settings remain instructor detail.
drafts.bridgeOut: With energy use, protection and measurement connected, return to the whole leaf's response to increasing light.

drafts.title: From photons to the light-response curve
drafts.bridgeIn: The light reactions explain why adding photons initially helps, then eventually produces diminishing returns.
drafts.takeaway: At low light, photons constrain photosynthesis; at higher light, downstream capacity increasingly limits their use.

context.heading: Read the curve from the mechanisms
paragraphs: At low absorbed photon flux, additional photons can drive additional productive photochemistry, so photosynthetic rate initially rises approximately linearly. The slope is a quantum yield only when its output and photon basis are specified—for example, moles of CO₂ assimilated per mole of incident or absorbed photons.

As irradiance increases, downstream processes cannot necessarily consume ATP and reducing power at the same rate as excitation arrives. The curve bends towards saturation while electron-flow regulation and heat dissipation become more important. A plateau does not mean pigments have stopped absorbing light, nor does it automatically imply photodamage.

A curve of net CO₂ exchange also includes carbon losses and can lie below zero at very low light. We will unpack those losses in the carbon lecture. Carbon metabolism is a sink that helps keep light-driven electron flow functioning.

study: Initial slope: quantum yield on a stated incident/absorbed photon basis.
Plateau: additional light no longer produces proportional carbon gain.
ATP/NADPH use links this curve to the carbon reactions.

history.title: Blackman's limiting factors
history.body: A short historical connection explains why a light-response curve cannot be understood from light absorption alone: increasing one input stops helping when another process limits the rate.

evidence.point: Modern route and carbon-metabolism studies strengthen the distinction between photon absorption, electron throughput and net carbon gain.
evidence.scope: No acclimation, temperature or drought-response lesson is added.

illustration.static: One explicitly labelled net CO₂ assimilation versus photon-flux curve. Mark the initial slope and saturation region, with a small ATP/NADPH arrow to carbon assimilation. Use a schematic curve unless actual data and measurement conditions are supplied.
illustration.animation: None needed.

optional: Leave detailed compensation-point interpretation for the gas-exchange slide in lecture 2.
If time is tight, the quantum-yield denominator matters more than extra curve-fitting parameters.
drafts.bridgeOut: Lecture 2 follows the products of the light reactions: how ATP and reducing power turn CO₂ into organic carbon.

drafts.title: From light energy to organic carbon
drafts.bridgeIn: The light reactions supplied ATP and NADPH on the stromal side of the thylakoid membrane.
drafts.takeaway: Carbon assimilation uses ATP and reducing power to build organic matter from CO₂.

context.heading: The two lectures describe one coupled system
paragraphs: CO₂ supplies carbon in a highly oxidised form. The Calvin–Benson–Bassham cycle uses NADPH as reducing power and ATP to drive the reactions that build and regenerate carbon intermediates. It occurs in the chloroplast stroma, beside the membrane system that supplies these currencies.

Using ATP and NADPH returns ADP, phosphate and NADP⁺ for reuse by the light reactions. Carbon assimilation is therefore not simply a product at the end of a one-way chain: it helps regenerate the acceptors that allow electron transfer to continue.

context.heading: Why 'dark reactions' is a misleading name
paragraphs: Carbon fixation does not require a photon at each enzymatic step, but in an ordinary illuminated leaf its energy supply and much of its regulation depend on light. Redox regulation coordinates several carbon-cycle enzymes with electron transport. The phrase 'dark reactions' does not mean that this cycle normally waits for night.

study: Stroma: CO₂ + ATP + reducing power → organic carbon.
ADP, phosphate and NADP⁺ return to the light reactions.
Carbon reactions are not restricted to darkness.

history.title: Light-independent chemistry is not nocturnal chemistry
history.body: The old terminology separates photochemical steps from enzymatic carbon reactions. Use it once to resolve the misconception, then call this the carbon-assimilation lecture.

evidence.point: Arabidopsis induction experiments link the redox state of selected carbon-cycle enzymes with electron-transport activation.
evidence.scope: A mechanistic connection, not an extra list of regulatory proteins or an acclimation topic.

illustration.static: Return to the opening photo/synthesis figure, now locating the thylakoid and stroma. Use a two-way exchange of ATP/NADPH and ADP/Pi/NADP⁺, plus CO₂ entering carbon metabolism.
illustration.animation: None needed.

optional: Rubisco activase can be mentioned later as an ATP-using maintenance/regulation function; its detailed mechanism is not required here.
drafts.bridgeOut: How was the route from invisible CO₂ into organic molecules discovered?

drafts.title: Following carbon into the Calvin–Benson–Bassham cycle
drafts.bridgeIn: We know what supplies the energy. To discover the carbon route, follow a labelled carbon atom.
drafts.takeaway: Rubisco adds CO₂ to a five-carbon acceptor, producing two three-carbon molecules.

context.heading: A tracer reveals the entry point
paragraphs: Calvin, Benson, Bassham and colleagues supplied photosynthesising cells with radiolabelled CO₂, stopped the reactions after short intervals and separated labelled compounds. Comparing early and later labelling revealed a pathway rather than merely measuring total sugar production.

At the entry to the C₃ cycle, Rubisco adds CO₂ to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, RuBP, a five-carbon acceptor. The transient six-carbon product yields two molecules of three-carbon 3-phosphoglycerate, 3-PGA. C₃ photosynthesis is named for this first stable fixation product, not for the eventual production of a three-carbon sugar.

context.heading: Begin with a count students can follow
paragraphs: For three CO₂ molecules, three RuBP molecules contribute fifteen existing carbons and the incoming CO₂ contributes three more. The result is six 3-PGA molecules, carrying eighteen carbons. The question is not only how to make reduced carbon from them, but also how to restore the acceptor so fixation can continue.
Rubisco's carboxylation reaction does not itself directly consume ATP or NADPH. Their expenditure becomes clear when we follow reduction and regeneration.

study: RuBP (5 C) + CO₂ (1 C) → 2 × 3-PGA (3 C).
For 3 CO₂: 3 RuBP → 6 3-PGA.
C₃ refers to the first stable fixation product.

history.title: Stop the reaction, then find the label
history.body: A short pulse of ¹⁴CO₂, rapid quenching and chromatographic separation turned a hidden metabolic route into a sequence of labelled compounds. Credit the research team, not Calvin alone.

evidence.point: A 2024 review marks seventy years since the cycle's general outline was published and explains how its products feed many pathways.
evidence.scope: The historical core remains sound; current work expands the metabolic connections rather than replacing carboxylation.

illustration.static: A small three-frame tracer experiment beside the carbon-count reaction. Use numbered carbon counts, not a complete enzyme chart.
illustration.animation: A brief tracer pulse could be part of the CBB sequence, but a static experiment strip is sufficient.

optional: A photograph of an original chromatogram can be linked as a source reference; do not reuse it without checking its licence and legibility.
The 1953 archived report and the 1954 journal paper are different publication records.
drafts.bridgeOut: Those six 3-PGA molecules must be reduced; most of the resulting carbon must then regenerate RuBP.

drafts.title: Reduction and regeneration keep the cycle running
drafts.bridgeIn: Three CO₂ have entered a pool of eighteen carbons. Only part of that carbon can leave if fixation is to continue.
drafts.takeaway: Most cycle carbon regenerates the CO₂ acceptor; one net triose phosphate leaves per three CO₂ fixed.

context.heading: ATP activates; NADPH reduces
paragraphs: For three CO₂ fixed, six molecules of 3-PGA are phosphorylated using six ATP and then reduced using six NADPH to form six triose phosphates. This is where reducing power from light-driven electron transfer changes the oxidation state of the carbon.

Triose phosphate is the useful three-carbon product pool. One net three-carbon equivalent can leave the cycle for biosynthesis; the remaining five triose-phosphate equivalents contain fifteen carbons.

context.heading: Regeneration closes the carbon balance
paragraphs: Through rearrangements of carbon skeletons, those fifteen carbons regenerate three five-carbon RuBP molecules. This regeneration phase consumes another three ATP. The acceptor pool is restored and can fix the next three CO₂.

The cycle is therefore not a chain that consumes one RuBP for every CO₂ forever. RuBP is continually regenerated, while external CO₂ supplies the net carbon gain. Exporting all six triose equivalents would empty the acceptor pool and stop further fixation.

study: 3 CO₂ → 6 3-PGA → 6 triose-phosphate equivalents.
One triose equivalent leaves; five regenerate three RuBP.
Reduction uses 6 ATP + 6 NADPH; regeneration uses 3 ATP.

history.title: The difficult part was closing the cycle
history.body: Identifying early labelled products was only the beginning. The 1954 work addressed how the CO₂ acceptor is regenerated, explaining sustained fixation without continually supplying a new acceptor.

evidence.point: Modern carbon-metabolism research retains these core transformations while examining flux into additional products and side pathways.
evidence.scope: Teach the canonical carbon count first; keep network extensions separate.

illustration.static: A restrained three-phase cycle with carbon-count groups: carboxylation, reduction, regeneration. Mark the one outgoing triose and five retained equivalents. ATP and NADPH inputs stay attached to their phases.
illustration.animation: Highest-priority carbon animation: 45–60 seconds moving carbon-count groups through the cycle. End on a static frame containing the complete balance.
illustration.priority: High: regeneration is hard to explain by speech alone

optional: Do not make students track every individual carbon position or all enzymes in this introductory slot.
Do not draw six triose products all leaving the cycle.
drafts.bridgeOut: The complete count tells us both the minimum energy demand and what 'making sugar' actually means.

drafts.title: What the cycle produces—and what it costs
drafts.bridgeIn: Reduction and regeneration together reveal the net output and the ATP/NADPH requirement.
drafts.takeaway: The canonical cycle makes one net triose phosphate from three CO₂ using nine ATP and six NADPH.

context.heading: Keep the accounting boundary visible
paragraphs: The canonical Calvin–Benson–Bassham account is 3 CO₂ → one net triose-phosphate equivalent, requiring 9 ATP and 6 NADPH. Per CO₂, that is 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, an ATP:NADPH demand ratio of 1.5. This count excludes photorespiration, CO₂-concentrating mechanisms and additional biosynthetic or maintenance costs.

Triose phosphate can support sucrose production outside the chloroplast or starch accumulation inside it, and also supplies carbon to other biosynthetic pathways. A six-carbon sugar equivalent requires two net three-carbon equivalents, but subsequent sugar synthesis and partitioning should not be mistaken for a direct glucose output from Rubisco.

context.heading: Return to the light-reaction budget
paragraphs: The ideal linear-flow example in lecture 1 supplied two NADPH with approximately 2.57 ATP under its stated coupling assumption. Comparing that with a 3 ATP:2 NADPH carbon demand shows why energy balance is a question worth asking.

The comparison alone does not prove that every leaf runs exactly the same additional cyclic flux. Demand changes with other metabolism; effective coupling and route regulation also matter. We now add an especially important change in demand: Rubisco can react with oxygen.

study: 3 CO₂ → 1 net triose phosphate.
9 ATP + 6 NADPH per net triose; 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂.
Further costs arise from photorespiration and concentrating mechanisms.

history.title: Do not add another historical detour
history.body: The carbon-count animation has already explained the cycle. Use this slide to consolidate the numbers and reconnect to ATP/NADPH supply.

evidence.point: Current reviews and flux work emphasise that photosynthetic carbon is distributed among multiple products, making whole-leaf demand broader than the isolated CBB cycle.
evidence.scope: The 9 ATP/6 NADPH core remains valid within its stated boundary.

illustration.static: One compact net-production account linked to modest sucrose/starch destinations. Beside it, compare carbon demand with the earlier illustrative light-reaction supply; keep both assumption labels visible.
illustration.animation: None needed.

optional: A worked 9-photon example combining linear flow with one extra non-pumping cyclic turn belongs in the accounting note, not another mandatory calculation.
drafts.bridgeOut: The oxygen made in the first lecture now returns as a competing substrate for the enzyme that fixes CO₂.

drafts.title: Rubisco reacts with CO₂—and O₂
drafts.bridgeIn: Rubisco connects incoming CO₂ with the carbon cycle, but its active site can also support an oxygenation reaction.
drafts.takeaway: Rubisco oxygenation creates a carbon-recovery problem that plants must solve.

context.heading: Two reactions from the same five-carbon substrate
paragraphs: Rubisco carboxylation produces two 3-PGA molecules from RuBP and CO₂. Oxygenation instead produces one 3-PGA and one two-carbon 2-phosphoglycolate, 2-PG. That second product cannot simply proceed through the ordinary reduction phase of the cycle and can interfere with metabolism if it accumulates.
The competition depends on the CO₂ and O₂ available at Rubisco and the enzyme's catalytic properties. Increasing CO₂ around Rubisco can therefore reduce the relative frequency of oxygenation.

Oxygenation does not release CO₂ directly at the Rubisco step. Carbon loss occurs later during recovery of the two-carbon product. Keeping those steps separate makes photorespiration and the C₂ concentrating mechanism easier to understand.

context.heading: Avoid the 'hopeless enzyme' story
paragraphs: Rubisco combines difficult chemistry with finite turnover and imperfect CO₂/O₂ discrimination. It is useful to teach those constraints, but calling it simply a badly designed, unchanged enzyme obscures evolution. Comparative work finds continuing changes in catalytic properties in plants.

Plants can respond at more than one level: by recovering carbon after oxygenation, by changing where that recovery releases CO₂, and by concentrating CO₂ before Rubisco reacts. These alternatives connect carbon recovery with CO₂ concentration.

study: Carboxylation: RuBP + CO₂ → 2 × 3-PGA.
Oxygenation: RuBP + O₂ → 3-PGA + 2-PG.
Oxygenation creates a salvage requirement; CO₂ release follows later.

history.title: The carboxylase was also an oxygenase
history.body: Bowes, Ogren and Hageman showed oxygen-dependent phosphoglycolate production by the purified enzyme in 1971, connecting Rubisco chemistry with the physiological puzzle of photorespiration.

evidence.point: A 2024 angiosperm analysis finds ongoing evolution in Rubisco kinetic properties and association with assimilation capacity.
evidence.scope: Comparative evidence, not a claim that all catalytic trade-offs disappear. A 2025 bacterial mutational map is further instructor context, not direct proof for crop Rubisco.

illustration.static: A single RuBP input branches into carboxylation and oxygenation with clearly counted products. Highlight 2-PG as the product requiring recovery. No enzyme cartoon implying conscious 'mistakes'.

drafts.title: Photorespiration recovers carbon at a cost
drafts.bridgeIn: Rubisco oxygenation leaves a two-carbon product outside the normal carbon-reduction route.
drafts.takeaway: Photorespiration salvages most of that carbon, while releasing CO₂ and requiring energy.

context.heading: Follow carbon across three organelles
paragraphs: In a typical land-plant leaf, recovery involves the chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion. Two molecules of 2-PG contain four carbons. After conversion through glycolate, glyoxylate and glycine, mitochondrial glycine decarboxylase and associated reactions convert two glycine molecules into serine, releasing one CO₂ and ammonia.

The three-carbon skeleton returns through glycerate to chloroplastic 3-PGA. In the canonical closed pathway, four carbons entering as two 2-PG are therefore recovered as three carbons in 3-PGA, with one carbon released as CO₂. This is a 25% loss from those two-carbon substrates, not a statement that every leaf always loses 25% of all photosynthesis.

Ammonia must be reassimilated and glycerate phosphorylated, so recovery consumes energy and reducing equivalents. Photorespiration is distinct from ordinary mitochondrial respiration and is active while photosynthesis proceeds.

context.heading: Salvage explains both its necessity and its cost
paragraphs: Without recovery, 2-PG would accumulate and carbon would be stranded outside the cycle. Photorespiration solves that problem, but it lowers net carbon gain relative to carboxylation alone. In the canonical account, each two oxygenations produce one photorespiratory CO₂ release: net carbon gain before other respiration is Vc − 0.5 Vo.

For a fully recycling carboxylation/oxygenation model, the combined demands can be written 3 Vc + 3.5 Vo ATP and 2 Vc + 2 Vo NADPH equivalents. These include restoring the carbon cycle after each reaction; they are not the cost of glycine decarboxylase alone. 'NADPH equivalents' is an electron account, not a claim that every organelle directly consumes NADPH.

Actual photorespiration is connected to wider metabolism: glycine, serine and one-carbon units can feed other pathways. That makes its physiological role richer than a pure waste loop, while also changing the canonical energy balance.

study: 2 × 2-PG (4 C) → 3-PGA (3 C) + CO₂ (1 C), through chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion.
Carbon and nitrogen recovery costs energy.
The position of glycine decarboxylation determines where CO₂ is released.

drafts.title: Evolution begins with CO₂ recapture
drafts.bridgeIn: Photorespiration releases CO₂ in mitochondria. The location of that release can change how much carbon escapes.
drafts.takeaway: Changes in cell organisation can improve CO₂ recapture before a complete C₄ cycle exists.

context.heading: Anatomy changes the chance of refixation
paragraphs: Photorespired CO₂ need not all leave the leaf. If mitochondria release it near chloroplasts containing Rubisco, some can be refixed. Changes in bundle-sheath organelle abundance and positioning can therefore improve carbon retention without first inventing an entirely new CO₂-fixing enzyme.

Proto-Kranz forms provide examples of anatomical arrangements intermediate between ordinary C₃ leaves and more specialised concentrating systems. These are useful for explaining how individually useful traits can accumulate, rather than imagining a fully integrated C₄ system appearing in one step.

context.heading: A narrative, not an inevitable ladder
paragraphs: Living C₃, C₂ and C₄ species let us compare mechanisms; they are not automatically direct ancestors and descendants. In some lineages, evidence supports a progression through enhanced photorespiratory recapture towards C₄. C₂ is also a functioning photosynthetic strategy in its own right, not necessarily an unfinished C₄ plant.

study: Photorespired CO₂ can be refixed before it escapes.
Bundle-sheath organisation can improve recapture.
C₃ → C₂ → C₄ is a useful lineage-supported narrative, not a universal destiny.

history.body: Anatomy, physiology and phylogeny together distinguish plausible transitions from a textbook ladder drawn after the fact.

drafts.bridgeIn: Anatomy can favour recapture. Relocating a key photorespiratory reaction makes that recapture more directed.
drafts.takeaway: The C₂ glycine shuttle concentrates photorespiratory CO₂ near bundle-sheath Rubisco.

context.heading: Move the two-carbon carrier before releasing CO₂
paragraphs: In C₂ photosynthesis, mesophyll photorespiration produces glycine, but glycine decarboxylation is strongly concentrated in bundle-sheath mitochondria. Glycine therefore moves towards the bundle sheath before its carbon is released.

There, two glycine molecules are converted through glycine decarboxylase and serine hydroxymethyltransferase into serine, CO₂ and ammonia. The released CO₂ is close to bundle-sheath Rubisco and can be recaptured. Serine and associated metabolites connect back to the recovery network. The name C₂ refers to the two-carbon glycine shuttle, not to a replacement two-carbon first product of ordinary CO₂ fixation.

context.heading: The crucial innovation is spatial organisation
paragraphs: C₂ does not require the full high-flux PEPC/C₄-acid cycle that defines C₄ photosynthesis. It changes where an existing photorespiratory reaction releases CO₂, reducing the chance of that carbon escaping. It can lower the CO₂ compensation point relative to comparable C₃ leaves, though the magnitude varies among species and conditions.

Recent molecular work makes this evolutionary idea concrete: in Brassicaceae, loss of mesophyll expression can reveal an already-existing bundle-sheath regulatory programme for glycine decarboxylase. A useful innovation can arise by redeploying existing biochemical machinery.

Bundle-sheath mitochondria: glycine → serine + CO₂.
Nearby Rubisco recaptures released CO₂; the full C₄ cycle is not required.

drafts.title: C₄ photosynthesis concentrates CO₂ before Rubisco
drafts.bridgeIn: C₂ concentrates CO₂ released by photorespiration. C₄ adds a high-flux concentrating cycle ahead of Rubisco.
drafts.takeaway: C₄ suppresses much oxygenation by concentrating CO₂, at an additional energy cost.

context.heading: An extra cycle around the same carbon-reduction chemistry
paragraphs: In a typical two-cell C₄ leaf, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, PEPC, fixes bicarbonate into a four-carbon product in mesophyll cells. Carbonic anhydrase connects incoming CO₂ with the bicarbonate substrate. C₄ acids such as malate or aspartate carry carbon towards the bundle sheath.

Decarboxylation releases CO₂ near Rubisco, raising its local CO₂ supply and reducing the relative frequency of oxygenation. The remaining three-carbon compound returns towards the mesophyll, where the CO₂ acceptor PEP is regenerated. The Calvin–Benson–Bassham cycle still performs carbon reduction; the C₄ cycle supplies a concentrating system around it.

context.heading: Concentration has a price
paragraphs: In the standard PPDK-based account, regenerating PEP consumes ATP to AMP, costing two high-energy phosphate equivalents per delivered CO₂. With no leakage and no photorespiratory cost, this adds approximately two ATP equivalents to the CBB baseline of three ATP and two NADPH per CO₂: an illustrative total of five ATP equivalents and two NADPH.

Real demand depends on leakage, pathway subtype and metabolite exchange between cell types. The ATP and reductant needs of the mesophyll and bundle sheath need not match each other. This reconnects directly to the flexible electron routes of lecture 1: proton-coupled cycling can matter especially in cells with high ATP demand.
C₄ is therefore not a replacement for Rubisco or a source of free extra carbon. It trades additional energy expenditure for a more favourable CO₂ environment around Rubisco.

study: PEPC fixes HCO₃⁻ in mesophyll → C₄ acid → CO₂ released near bundle-sheath Rubisco.
The CBB cycle remains the carbon-reduction pathway.
Illustrative extra cost: 2 ATP equivalents per concentrated CO₂, before leakage.

context.heading: Store at night, release by day
paragraphs: In the standard CAM pattern, nocturnal PEPC fixation supplies organic acids that accumulate in vacuoles. During the day, decarboxylation supplies CO₂ to the Calvin–Benson–Bassham cycle while stomata can remain relatively closed. The same basic distinction remains: an initial concentrating/storage pathway supports subsequent Rubisco carboxylation and carbon reduction.

C₄ and CAM are often introduced as spatial and temporal separation, respectively. That comparison is useful, provided it is not treated as a rigid rule that the two strategies can never coexist. Some Portulaca species combine C₄ with inducible CAM features.

drafts.title: What a leaf's CO₂ exchange measures
drafts.bridgeIn: Carboxylation gains carbon, while photorespiration and other metabolism can release it at the same time.
drafts.takeaway: Net assimilation is the balance of carbon gain and simultaneous carbon losses.

context.heading: A chamber sees the net balance
paragraphs: A leaf gas-exchange chamber compares CO₂ entering and leaving at a known flow, with the necessary dilution corrections. This estimates the leaf's net CO₂ uptake; it does not directly count Rubisco turnovers.

For a conventional C₃ steady-state account, A = Vc − 0.5 Vo − Rᴸ: Rubisco carboxylation minus photorespiratory CO₂ release and other CO₂ release in the light. The 0.5 factor comes from the two-oxygenation carbon-recovery account. Rᴸ is often called day respiration, but it should not be defined as necessarily all, or only, mitochondrial respiration.
A net rate of zero does not imply that carboxylation has stopped. At a compensation point, gains and losses balance. This also explains why the light-response curve can cross zero.

context.heading: The enzyme experiences chloroplastic CO₂
paragraphs: CO₂ moves from ambient air, Ca, through stomata to intercellular airspaces, Ci, and then through mesophyll diffusion pathways to the chloroplast, Cc. A measured A–Ci curve is therefore not automatically a direct Rubisco response to Ci: the biochemical model's CO₂ substrate is Cc.
Diffusion and biochemical consumption jointly determine the CO₂ available to Rubisco.

study: A = Vc − 0.5 Vo − Rᴸ in the canonical C₃ account.
Ca → Ci → Cc; Rubisco experiences Cc.

history.title: Gas exchange connects biochemistry to an intact leaf
history.body: The value of the measurement is that it tests the combined biochemical account in a living leaf. This is the immediate motivation for the FvCB model.

evidence.point: A recent review uses isotope and flux evidence to reconsider the metabolic origins of CO₂ release in the light, including non-mitochondrial routes.
evidence.scope: Use Rᴸ as a measured/modelled non-photorespiratory release term without claiming one source dominates all species and conditions.

drafts.title: FvCB links carbon fixation to energy supply
drafts.bridgeIn: Net exchange combines several fluxes. A useful model asks which process can support the lowest carboxylation capacity.
drafts.takeaway: FvCB connects Rubisco capacity, RuBP regeneration and carbon loss in one biochemical model.

context.heading: Two capacities organise the first explanation
paragraphs: Rubisco can fix CO₂ only as fast as its catalytic capacity allows and only as fast as its acceptor, RuBP, is regenerated. In the basic FvCB picture, carboxylation is constrained by the smaller of these capacities. At low chloroplastic CO₂, the Rubisco-limited branch often controls the response; at higher CO₂ under a fixed light supply, regeneration can become limiting.

Vcmax represents a maximum Rubisco carboxylation capacity. J represents electron supply supporting the regeneration account, and Jmax is a capacity parameter for its light response. Subtracting photorespiratory and other CO₂ release gives the observable net assimilation A. This brings both lectures together: the light reactions supply energy, and carbon metabolism determines how it can be used.

context.heading: Keep the meaning of the quantities clear
paragraphs: For the usual reductant-based regeneration expression, Aj = J(Cc − Γ*)/[4(Cc + 2Γ*)] − Rᴸ. Cc is chloroplastic CO₂ and Γ* is the photorespiratory compensation point without Rᴸ. The denominator accounts for electron requirements of carboxylation and oxygenation; it is not simply an empirical curve shape.

J in that expression is not automatically the total PSII ETR estimated from fluorescence. Alternative sinks and different ATP/reductant coupling assumptions change the connection. That is why the flexible electron-routing discussion belongs before the model rather than being treated as an optional afterthought.

FvCB is a compact steady-state biochemical model, not a full simulation of induction, protection and every metabolic pathway. A further limitation can arise when the capacity to use triose phosphate constrains carbon metabolism; this is an extension of the basic two-capacity account.

study: Carboxylation is constrained by Rubisco capacity or RuBP-regeneration capacity.
Vcmax: Rubisco capacity. J/Jmax: usable electron supply and its capacity.
